title: Cap. 6 preliminaries: No fixed law that good use of nature buys supernatural light
pass_a_gloss: I will premise a few things, then I will come to confirming the thesis. First therefore it is to be observed that those constituted in the contrary sentence think God obligated as if by a fixed decree and statute-law to impart the talent of grace to those using well the talent of nature. Second, they presume that any Pagan human whatsoever, even sitting in the shadow of death, can by the liberty of his will use this natural talent well or badly. Third, from this discrimination of those using natural gifts rightly or otherwise, they try to render the cause why God deigns to illuminate certain ones with the Gospel and the knowledge of Christ, and does not deign to illuminate others. If anyone uses those gifts rightly, they state that he is to be led little by little into saving knowledge of Christ: but if he abusively abuses them, then they say he is deservedly deprived of the knowledge of Christ. Augustine seems to have been constituted in the contrary sentence, in the book De Natura et Gratia, chapters 8 and 9. Where he concedes that to certain infants the media of salvation could not have been applied; where he also acknowledges that adults who died in that region where they could not hear the name of Christ could in no way have become just through nature and free choice. We also affirm that no decree, no law or promise of God exists, according to which anyone could certainly conclude: This human has used natural light rightly or less badly, therefore God will illuminate him with supernatural grace. Arminius indeed says that God pledged this by that saying of Christ, TO THE ONE WHO HAS IT WILL BE GIVEN. But far more truly and learnedly the Reverend of Salisbury: Arminius hints a fallacy here, and commits it, who by a leap promises to the one who has in the state of nature a gift in the state of grace, and makes the light of faith the wage of the diligence of unbelievers. For what is in the matter, and in what genus the use is, in the same also increment is promised. Alvarez, a Pontifical man, votes with us in this matter: No law was ever established about giving helps of grace to those doing the whole of what is in them from the faculty of nature; nor did Christ the Lord by his death merit, or will to merit, such a law. The Apostle Paul teaches that the dispensation of supernatural grace proceeds not according to the use and works of the human will, but according to the purpose and counsel of the divine will: He works all things according to the purpose and counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11).
pass_b_english: A few preliminaries, then I turn to confirming the thesis. First, notice that those on the opposite side think God is bound by a fixed decree and statute to give the talent of grace to those who use the talent of nature well. Second, they presume that any pagan, even one sitting in the shadow of death, can by free choice use that natural talent well or badly. Third, from that difference between those who use natural gifts rightly and those who do not, they try to explain why God deigns to light some with the gospel and the knowledge of Christ and does not deign to light others. Use the gifts rightly, they say, and the person is gradually to be led into saving knowledge of Christ; abuse them wickedly, and he is justly stripped of that knowledge.

Augustine seems to stand on the opposite side in De Natura et Gratia, chapters 8 and 9. There he grants that for certain infants the means of salvation could not be applied; and he also owns that adults who died in a region where they could not hear Christ’s name could in no way become just by nature and free choice. We likewise affirm that no decree, law, or promise of God exists by which anyone could safely conclude: this person used natural light rightly, or less badly; therefore God will illuminate him with supernatural grace.

Arminius does say God pledged this by Christ’s word, “To the one who has, it will be given” (Matthew 13:12). But the Reverend of Salisbury speaks more truly and more learnedly: Arminius hints a fallacy here, and commits it—leaping from the one who has in the state of nature to a gift in the state of grace, and making the light of faith the wage of unbelievers’ diligence. For what is promised, and in what kind the use falls, is increase in that same kind. Alvarez, a Roman Catholic writer, votes with us here: no law was ever enacted that helps of grace must be given to those who do all that is in them from nature’s faculty; nor did the Lord Christ by his death merit, or will to merit, such a law. The Apostle Paul teaches that the dispensation of supernatural grace runs not according to the use and works of the human will, but according to the purpose and counsel of the divine will: “He works all things according to the purpose and counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11).
source_text: Paucula praemittam, dein ad thesin confirmandam accedam. Primo igitur observandum est, in contraria sententia constitutos putare, Deum quasi fixo decreto ac statuta lege obligatum, ut bene utentibus talento naturae impertiat talentum gratiae. Secundo, praesumunt quemlibet hominem Paganum, etiam in umbra mortis sedentem, posse pro libertate voluntatis suae bene aut male uti hoc talento naturali. Tertio, ab hoc discrimine recte aut secus utentium donis naturalibus, causam reddere conantur, cur Deus quosdam dignetur Evangelio & cognitione Christi illustrare, alios non dignetur. Si quis recte donis illis utatur, hunc paulatim ducendum statuunt in salutiferam Christi cognitionem: Si vero improbe illis abutatur, tum dicunt illum merito privari cognitione Christi. Augustinus videtur in contraria sententia fuisse constitutus, libro de Nat. & Gratia, cap. 8. & 9. Ubi quibusdam infantibus media salutis applicari non potuisse concedit; ubi etiam agnoscit adultos in ea regione defunctos ubi non potuerunt Christi nomen audire, per naturam & liberum arbitrium justos fieri nullo modo potuisse. Nos etiam affirmamus, nullum decretum, nullam Dei legem aut promissionem exstare, juxta quam certo quis posset concludere, Hic homo recte aut minus male usus est lumine naturali, ergo Deus illuminabit eum gratia supernaturali. Dicit quidem Arminius, Deum hoc spopondisse isto Christi dicto, HABENTI DABITUR. Sed multo verius & doctius Reverendus Sarisburiensis, Fallaciam innuit, hic committit Arminius, qui habenti in statu naturae per saltum promittit donum in statu gratiae, & incredulorum diligentiae lucem fidei mercedem facit. Nam quod in re, & quo in genere usus, in eodem quoque incrementum promittitur. Alvarez homo Pontificius nobis hac in re suffragatur, Nulla lex fuit unquam statuta de dandis auxiliis gratiae, facientibus totum quod in se est ex facultate naturae; neque Christus Dominus morte sua meruit, aut mereri voluit talem legem. Apostolus Paulus dispensationem gratiae supernaturalis procedere docet, non secundum usum & opera voluntatis humanae, sed secundum propositum & consilium voluntatis Divinae: Operator omnia secundum propositum & consilium voluntatis suae, Ephes. i. 11.
